name: Release State Check
description: Paste a dataset DOI and see whether the release behind it has been published or only announced: does it resolve, does its registry have a public record, which version does the record name, and is a newer record linked — read live, with the time of the read.
data_source: Live public reads of doi.org (resolver and agency lookup), the DataCite public API and the Crossref public API, made from the visitor's browser; two worked reads of public dataset surfaces dated 2026-11-11
records: 0 stored records; each check is a live read. 2 worked reads with dated receipts
detail: Static client-side reader. Reports one of: not registered; registered with no public record (the state a DOI is in when created ahead of release or withdrawn from listing); public record; public record that names a newer one; public record with a publisher update notice attached; unknown when a source fails to answer — an error is never shown as a state. Also flags a DOI that points at a site's front page instead of a dataset page, a record with no version field, differing addresses, and a record that is one version under a parent. A method page gives three delivery-side checks the page cannot do (read the download form, compare a refused file with sibling datasets on the same host, compare a window before trusting a mirror) and two worked reads. A standard-library Python script provides the same reader and the sibling-host comparison for the command line. Reads DataCite and Crossref only; never requests a data file; not a monitor.
asymmetry: Whoever holds the working copy or the current vintage benefits from the gap between what a public catalogue advertises and what the download site serves. A reseller can sell 'current' access while the public path stalls, and an identifier created ahead of release reads as 'published' in every citation that carries it. A planner, researcher, journalist or small-firm analyst deciding whether to wait, cite, buy access or give up cannot tell 'not yet published' from 'published and not served' — both look like an empty portal.
pipeline_note: No pipeline. Reading rules are pure functions in core.js with a Python twin in check.py; 18 recorded and synthetic source answers plus 11 host cases run through both and must agree. Playwright smoke (sources answered from the same case file; dated header, deep links, unknown-on-failure, markup escaping, 390px width, no requests outside the three sources) run on the staged deploy and the live URL. Worked reads carry a receipts file of addresses and statuses.
